interactions.label: A woman from an iodine-deficient region with long-standing multinodular goitre i

params.question: A woman from an iodine-deficient region with long-standing multinodular goitre is started on iodine supplementation. Within weeks she develops palpitations, weight loss, and sweating. Her TSH is undetectable. What is the most likely mechanism?

answers.text: Autoimmune thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins cross-activate the TSH receptor persistently

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TSI-driven activation is the mechanism in Graves disease, not in toxic multinodular goitre. Toxic MNG arises from clonal autonomous nodules, not from autoimmunity.

answers.text: Sudden iodine availability fuels autonomous nodules that produce hormone without TSH stimulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the Jod-Basedow phenomenon. Autonomous nodules in long-standing MNG no longer require TSH; when iodine — their only missing substrate — is restored, they produce excess hormone, precipitating thyrotoxicosis.

answers.text: Excess iodine inhibits thyroid peroxidase via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, causing a rebound hormone surge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Wolff-Chaikoff effect suppresses synthesis and causes hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism. It is not the mechanism behind the Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

answers.text: Iodine supplementation raises T4, stimulating the pituitary to secrete more TSH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rising T4 suppresses TSH via negative feedback — the opposite of what this option states. In Jod-Basedow, TSH is undetectable because autonomous hormone production is entirely TSH-independent.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Jod-Basedow phenomenon describes thyrotoxicosis triggered when sudden iodine availability fuels autonomous nodules in long-standing multinodular goitre — distinct from the autoimmune mechanism of Graves disease and the opposite of the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

Correct. Jod-Basedow occurs when iodine repletion arms autonomous nodules in substrate-starved MNG, causing thyrotoxicosis. This is why iodine supplementation must be introduced gradually in endemic goitre populations.

params.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with palpitations, weight loss, and bilateral exophthalmos. Her TSH is undetectable and radioactive iodine uptake is diffusely elevated. Which mechanism best explains her thyroid overactivity?

answers.text: Cytotoxic CD8-positive T cells destroy follicular cells, releasing stored thyroid hormone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CD8-mediated follicular destruction characterises Hashimoto thyroiditis, which ends in hypothyroidism. In thyroiditis, RAIU is suppressed — passive hormone leakage, not active synthesis, drives transient thyrotoxicosis.

answers.text: IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind and persistently activate the TSH receptor, escaping negative feedback

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In Graves disease, TSI mimic TSH but are not regulated by rising thyroid hormone levels. This unregulated receptor activation drives excess T3/T4 synthesis — explaining diffuse high RAIU. TSI also cross-react with TSH receptors on orbital fibroblasts, causing exophthalmos.

answers.text: Viral follicular rupture spills colloid into surrounding tissue, triggering granulomatous inflammation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Follicular rupture with granulomas describes De Quervain (subacute) thyroiditis. RAIU is suppressed in that condition because passive leakage, not active synthesis, causes the transient thyrotoxic phase.

answers.text: Autonomous clonal nodules produce hormone without TSH signalling after repeated hyperplasia-involution cycles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Autonomous nodules describe toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease). RAIU in that condition is patchy, not diffuse. Bilateral exophthalmos is a specific extrathyroidal feature of Graves disease, not of toxic MNG.

overallFeedback.feedback: Diffuse elevated RAIU with bilateral exophthalmos points to Graves disease, where IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor independently of negative feedback — distinguishing it from viral thyroiditis, Hashimoto disease, and toxic MNG.

Correct. TSI in Graves disease persistently activate the TSH receptor outside normal feedback control, producing diffuse high RAIU and thyrotoxicosis. Ophthalmopathy results from TSI cross-reacting with TSH receptors on orbital fibroblasts.

params.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a heart rate of 50 beats per minute, periorbital puffiness, and deep tendon reflexes that are brisk on strike but disproportionately slow to relax. Her serum TSH is 85 mIU/L. Which diagnosis best explains this picture?

answers.text: Graves disease — thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins drive autonomous TSH-receptor overactivation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism: tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, and fast-relaxing reflexes. TSH is suppressed, not elevated to 85 mIU/L.

answers.text: Primary hypothyroidism — thyroid hormone deficiency slowing metabolic and neurological function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Elevated TSH confirms primary thyroid failure. The hallmark sign here is the hung-up reflex — brisk contraction followed by disproportionately delayed relaxation — caused by slowed muscle metabolism from thyroid hormone deficiency.

answers.text: Toxic multinodular goitre — autonomous nodule production overwhelming feedback suppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Toxic MNG causes hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH, not elevated TSH. Signs would include tachycardia and fast-relaxing reflexes, not bradycardia and the hung-up reflex.

answers.text: De Quervain thyroiditis — active granulomatous phase with passive hormone leakage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The thyrotoxic phase of De Quervain thyroiditis causes transient hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH. This patient's TSH of 85 mIU/L indicates chronic primary thyroid failure, not a self-limited post-viral thyroiditis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The hung-up reflex (disproportionately delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes) is pathognomonic of hypothyroidism. TSH of 85 mIU/L confirms primary thyroid failure — the opposite of what hyperthyroid conditions produce.

Correct. The hung-up reflex — brisk contraction with prolonged relaxation — is the hallmark sign of hypothyroidism. Combined with bradycardia and markedly elevated TSH, it confirms primary thyroid failure.

interactions.label: Fine needle aspiration cytology of a thyroid nodule shows optically clear nuclei

params.question: Fine needle aspiration cytology of a thyroid nodule shows optically clear nuclei with chromatin displaced to the nuclear periphery, linear infoldings of the nuclear membrane, and concentrically laminated calcifications. Which diagnosis do these features establish?

answers.text: Follicular thyroid carcinoma — diagnosed by capsular or vascular invasion on histology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Follicular carcinoma cannot be diagnosed on cytology; follicular carcinoma and follicular adenoma are cytologically identical. The defining criterion — capsular or vascular invasion — requires a histological section of the entire tumour.

answers.text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma — Orphan Annie nuclei, nuclear grooves, pseudoinclusions, and psammoma bodies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The nuclear triad of optically clear (Orphan Annie) nuclei, nuclear grooves, and pseudoinclusions — together with psammoma bodies — is near-pathognomonic for papillary thyroid carcinoma and can establish the diagnosis on FNAC alone.

answers.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma — polygonal C-cell nests with amyloid stroma and elevated serum calcitonin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and shows amyloid stroma between tumour nests. It does not display Orphan Annie nuclei or psammoma bodies; the serum marker is calcitonin, not a cytological finding.

answers.text: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma — highly pleomorphic cells with TP53 mutation and absent follicular differentiation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anaplastic carcinoma shows frankly pleomorphic, undifferentiated cells, not the clear grooved nuclei of papillary carcinoma. It occurs almost exclusively after age 65 and carries a median survival of 3–6 months.

overallFeedback.feedback: Optically clear (Orphan Annie) nuclei, nuclear grooves, nuclear pseudoinclusions, and psammoma bodies are the hallmarks of papillary thyroid carcinoma — the only thyroid malignancy diagnosable on cytology without demonstrating capsular invasion.

Correct. The Orphan Annie nucleus, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies together are near-pathognomonic for papillary thyroid carcinoma on FNAC — the only thyroid carcinoma diagnosable on cytology alone without needing histological capsular assessment.

interactions.label: A 40-year-old man presents with a thyroid mass and markedly elevated serum calci

params.question: A 40-year-old man presents with a thyroid mass and markedly elevated serum calcitonin. Biopsy shows polygonal cell nests surrounded by amyloid stroma. Germline RET mutation testing is positive. What is the most critical next step for his first-degree relatives?

answers.text: Annual thyroid ultrasound surveillance for all relatives, beginning at age 18

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ultrasound surveillance is insufficient — hereditary medullary carcinoma from RET mutations develops in early childhood. Waiting until age 18 risks missing the curative window entirely.

answers.text: RET genetic testing followed by prophylactic thyroidectomy for mutation-positive relatives before age five

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Germline RET mutations (MEN2A, MEN2B) cause hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma. The standard of care is RET testing of all first-degree relatives; mutation carriers receive prophylactic thyroidectomy before age five to prevent an aggressive and lethal malignancy.

answers.text: Radioiodine ablation for all relatives with elevated serum calcitonin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, not follicular cells, and does not concentrate radioiodine. Radioiodine ablation has no role in medullary carcinoma management.

answers.text: TSH suppression therapy with levothyroxine for all first-degree relatives

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TSH suppression benefits differentiated thyroid cancers (papillary and follicular) that are TSH-responsive. Medullary carcinoma is TSH-independent and does not respond to levothyroxine suppression.

overallFeedback.feedback: A germline RET mutation defines hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma within MEN2. All first-degree relatives need RET testing; mutation carriers receive prophylactic thyroidectomy before age five — not surveillance, not radioiodine, and not TSH suppression.

Correct. Hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma from germline RET mutations (MEN2A/2B) mandates genetic testing of all first-degree relatives; mutation-positive carriers receive prophylactic thyroidectomy before age five.

params.question: A 62-year-old woman is found incidentally to have serum calcium of 11.9 mg/dL. She reports recurrent renal calculi, vague bone pain, constipation, and mild confusion. Intact PTH is markedly elevated. Which pathology accounts for 85 percent of such primary cases?

answers.text: Chief cell hyperplasia involving all four parathyroid glands

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Four-gland chief cell hyperplasia accounts for approximately 14 percent of primary hyperparathyroidism, not 85 percent. Involvement of all four glands is also the hallmark of secondary hyperparathyroidism.

answers.text: Solitary parathyroid adenoma — autonomous chief cell proliferation with a compressed rim of normal gland at the periphery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A parathyroid adenoma causes 85 percent of primary hyperparathyroidism. Its pathological hallmark is the compressed rim of normal parathyroid tissue at the edge, along with absent intracellular fat — distinguishing it from a hyperplastic gland.

answers.text: Parathyroid carcinoma producing elevated PTH-related protein alongside intact PTH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Parathyroid carcinoma accounts for less than 1 percent of primary hyperparathyroidism. Elevated PTHrP points towards malignancy or a non-parathyroid source of hypercalcaemia, not the common adenoma.

answers.text: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism — autonomous gland function following prolonged chronic kidney disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism requires a prior history of secondary HPT from chronic kidney disease. It does not present as an incidental finding in an otherwise well patient; all four glands are autonomous, not a single adenoma.

overallFeedback.feedback: Primary hyperparathyroidism is caused by a parathyroid adenoma in 85 percent of cases. The clinical tetrad — renal calculi, bone pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, and neuropsychiatric features — is captured by the mnemonic: stones, bones, groans, and psychic moans.

Correct. A solitary parathyroid adenoma causes 85 percent of primary hyperparathyroidism. The clinical picture follows the mnemonic: stones (renal calculi), bones (bone pain), groans (constipation, peptic ulcer), and psychic moans (confusion, fatigue).
